description: Interactive, privacy-preserving demonstrations of evidence-reviewed cognitive bias effects. These demos do not collect responses and are not scientific measurements.

entries.title: Does the First Number Pull Your Estimate?
entries.summary: Try two versions of the same pricing question and see why a starting number can pull later estimates toward it.
entries.researchQuestion: Can an arbitrary starting price shift a later estimate even when the product information stays the same?

conditions.label: Higher anchor
conditions.prompt: A used laptop is in good condition, three years old, with 16 GB RAM and 512 GB storage. The seller asks €1,500. What price would you consider fair?

conditions.label: Lower anchor
conditions.prompt: A used laptop is in good condition, three years old, with 16 GB RAM and 512 GB storage. The seller asks €700. What price would you consider fair?

entries.prediction: Across groups, estimates often move toward the starting number. One person's answer cannot establish an anchoring effect.
entries.interpretation: The useful comparison is not whether €700 or €1,500 is a good price. It is whether changing only the starting number changes the later estimate.
entries.debias: Build an independent estimate from comparable products, budget and requirements before looking at the seller's target.

entries.title: Does Survival vs Mortality Wording Change the Feeling?
entries.summary: The numbers stay identical while the wording changes from survival to mortality. Notice whether your evaluation moves with the frame.
entries.researchQuestion: Can equivalent outcome statistics feel different when they are described as survival rather than mortality?
entries.responseLabel: How reassuring does this result feel? 1 = not reassuring, 7 = very reassuring

conditions.label: Survival frame
conditions.prompt: After one year, 90 out of 100 patients who receive Treatment A are alive.

conditions.label: Mortality frame
conditions.prompt: Within one year, 10 out of 100 patients who receive Treatment A die.

entries.prediction: Equivalent outcomes can receive different evaluations when one version highlights survival and the other highlights mortality.
entries.interpretation: The underlying numbers are the same. The demonstration asks whether a change in presentation changes your evaluation.
entries.debias: Restate important outcomes in both gain and loss terms before comparing options.

entries.title: Can a Third Option Change Which Plan You Prefer?
entries.summary: Choose between two plans, then compare the same choice after a clearly weaker third option appears.
entries.researchQuestion: Can an inferior comparison option change preference between two original alternatives?

conditions.label: Two-option menu
conditions.prompt: You need cloud storage for one year. Which plan would you choose?

conditions.label: Menu with a decoy
conditions.prompt: You need cloud storage for one year. Which plan would you choose?

entries.prediction: Adding an option that is clearly worse than Pro at the same price can make Pro easier to justify, even though Basic and Pro did not change.
entries.interpretation: The interesting variable is the choice set. If preference changes after adding the weak Plus option, the comparison structure is doing work.
entries.debias: Remove any option you would never choose and compare the remaining alternatives on your actual needs.

entries.title: Would You Continue If the Past Investment Disappeared?
entries.summary: The future economics stay the same. Only one version reminds you how much has already been spent.
entries.researchQuestion: Does visible past investment make continued funding feel more attractive even when future costs and benefits are unchanged?

conditions.label: Past investment visible
conditions.prompt: A project has already used €400,000 and eight months of work. From today, it needs another €100,000. There is a 30% chance it will produce €250,000 of future business value. Continue or stop?

conditions.label: Future-only version
conditions.prompt: A project starts today. It needs €100,000. There is a 30% chance it will produce €250,000 of future business value. Continue or stop?

entries.prediction: Past investment can increase willingness to continue even though those costs cannot improve the future payoff.
entries.interpretation: The future decision is identical in both versions. The €400,000 has already gone and should not become a future benefit.
entries.debias: Ask whether you would fund the next step if the project arrived today with no history.

entries.title: Does the Outcome Change How Good the Decision Looks?
entries.summary: Rate the same decision process after either a lucky or unlucky result.
entries.researchQuestion: Can knowing the outcome change how people judge the quality of the earlier decision process?
entries.responseLabel: How good was the original decision? 1 = very poor, 7 = very good

conditions.label: Good outcome
conditions.prompt: A manager compared three suppliers, checked financial stability, references and delivery performance, then chose the strongest option. A rare disruption did not occur and delivery succeeded.

conditions.label: Bad outcome
conditions.prompt: A manager compared three suppliers, checked financial stability, references and delivery performance, then chose the strongest option. A rare disruption occurred and delivery failed.

entries.prediction: The same process may be judged more harshly after a bad outcome and more positively after a good one.
entries.interpretation: A good process can have a bad result under uncertainty, and a weak process can sometimes get lucky. Review both separately.
entries.debias: Score the decision using only information available before the outcome, then review the result as a separate learning signal.

entries.title: What Happens When You See the Reference Class?
entries.summary: Estimate a project from the inside view, then compare it with a version that includes how long similar work actually took.
entries.researchQuestion: Does adding a reference class change a delivery estimate built from an ideal step-by-step plan?

conditions.label: Inside view
conditions.prompt: A team must migrate 30 reports. The plan is: export, transform, load, test, review. Assuming normal availability, how many working days will it take?

conditions.label: Outside view added
conditions.prompt: A team must migrate 30 reports. The plan is: export, transform, load, test, review. The last eight comparable migrations took a median of 18 working days, with a range of 14–27 days. How many working days will this one take?

entries.prediction: A reference class often shifts estimates away from the clean internal plan and toward outcomes seen in comparable completed work.
entries.interpretation: This is also an intervention demo: the outside view does not prove your first estimate was biased, but it adds evidence the inside view can miss.
entries.debias: Start with comparable completed work, then explain why the current case should be faster or slower.
